title: Compact task folding and deep-link failovers — notes
body:
Purpose
---
Capture experimental notes + wireframe writeups for a compact sidebar (task-folding) approach that preserves deep-link resiliency and predictable fallbacks when routes are missing or user state is incompatible. This doc is intentionally practical: sketches, acceptance criteria, visible failure modes, and groomed backlog items (with suggested priorities).

Context / why this matters
---
- Console growth -> more surface area (models, routes, deployments, keys). Full left nav can't scale without overwhelming vertical space.
- Users want shallow, repeatable entry points (deep links from alerts, docs, CI). If a route or resource moves, we must fail gracefully and surface a clear escape.
- Compact/keyboard-first views are high-value for power users (SREs/Platform engineers) who want density + quick navigation.

Design goals (measurable)
---
1) Deep-link resiliency: 90% of incoming deep links either load the target or redirect to a contextual landing with CTA to recover.
2) Discoverability: new compact mode should retain discovery for 80% of top tasks via progressive reveal.
3) Low-friction fallback: when resource not found, show suggested alternatives (recent items, related model families) within 300ms.
4) Accessibility: full keyboard nav and ARIA landmarks; compact mode must not reduce screen reader clarity.

Personas in focus
---
- Platform Engineer (keyboard-first, uses kanban/CLI alerts)
- Product PM (navigates via deep links from tickets)
- Solutions Engineer (often on laptop, toggles between routes quickly)

Wireframe variations (textual writeups)
---
1) Folded Task Column (FT Column)
- Left-most column is a narrow rail (56px) showing icon stack (homes, routes, monitor, models, keys). Hover/expand reveals a secondary slab (overlay) with contextual actions and previews.
- When a task is opened, instead of pushing full page, a mid-density task sheet slides over center (not full width) preserving vertical context. Sheet has a small header crumb with route id and a copyable deep-link.
- Deep-link behavior: if resource exists, open sheet and highlight; if not, transform sheet into "recovery mode" with suggestions (recent same-type items + link to search).
- Pros: space-efficient, retains glanceable icons. Cons: hover-reveal discoverability risk; requires clear keyboard affordances.

2) Stacked Context Pane (SCP)
- Left rail contains grouped task clusters (e.g., Observability, Models, Deploy). Clicking group expands an accordion in-place (inline expansion) rather than navigating.
- Deep links attempt to focus the correct group and open the specific item in the stack. If the item is archived or permission-denied, the stack shows a soft-error row with actionable CTA (request access, open ticket, revert to previous version).
- Pros: clear group semantics; non-modal. Cons: deep stacks can lead to long scroll — introduce a sticky mini-search.

3) Route-Resilient Landing + Smart Redirect (RRLSR)
- Minimal changes to rail; instead implement a smart landing page that is the universal target for ambiguous deep links. Landing shows: resolved path, probable alternatives, and a one-click recover (open most-recent matching item).
- Route resolution algorithm: exact-match => load; fuzzy-match (name/id mismatch) => show alternatives; permission-failure => show request-access flow; 404 => show search with filters pre-populated.
- Pros: simple nav change; centralized fallback UX. Cons: adds an extra hop for exact matches unless optimized.

Accessibility and keyboard patterns
---
- All hover reveals must have keyboard equivalents (e.g., Tab on rail icon opens expand state).
- ARIA: rail role=navigation; each group role=region with aria-labelledby.
- Deep-link copyable element must be focusable with label "Copy deep link" and keyboard shortcut (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+C).
- Visual focus indicator must be >=3px and high-contrast (WCAG AA+).

Failure modes and observed behaviors (from testing notes)
---
- Flaky route resolution under high load: when backend route index delayed, deep-link opens landing but shows stale alternatives. Mitigation: client-side cache + optimistic UI for 200ms window.
- Hover-only discoverability leads to confusion in tests where participants never found an action; make expand on focus mandatory.
- Permission-driven redirects are a common source of lost context: users lose the original query params. Fix: preserve query params and surface masked results with explainers.

Decision log (quick)
---
- 2024-09-16: prefer FT Column + RRLSR hybrid (compact rail + centralized landing) — cheaper rollout and incremental. (Decision maker: Ava, Mateo)
- 2024-09-24: require keyboard-on-focus reveal for all hover interactions. (Accessibility review: Sofia)

Groomed backlog (short)
---
- RW-4521: Implement compact rail primitives (icons + focus expansion) — P0 for alpha. Notes: need animation budget + reduced repaint. (owner: frontend)
- RW-4522: Deep-link resolver service: publish fuzzy-match API + popularity scoring — P0. (owner: infra)
- RW-4789: Landing page prototype with suggested alternatives and recover CTA — P1. (owner: product)
- RW-4820: Accessibility acceptance tests for compact mode (keyboard + screen reader) — P0. (owner: qa)
- RW-4890: Instrumentation: time-to-redirect, time-to-suggest; add tracing tags for resolution flow — P1. (owner: observability)
- TODO: add e2e scenario for permission denied deep-link (simulate SSO denial + fallback messaging). (RW task TBD)

Prototype interaction notes (for engineers)
---
- Keep rail stateless where possible: render icons client-side; expansion state transient in memory, not URL-driven (except when user explicitly pins).
- Deep links should be canonicalized: /models/{id} and /models/{id}?v=sha -> resolver returns canonical and an alias list. On mismatch, client updates URL with replaceState to avoid polluting history.
- For sheet mode, use CSS containment and will-change on transform to limit layout thrash.

Testing checklist (usability + perf)
---
- Usability: 6 participants, mixed-power novices, measure time-to-target for 5 deep-link tasks.
- Perf: under cold start, route resolution < 150ms 90p; under load (500rps) < 300ms 75p.
- Accessibility: axe + manual SR test on macOS VoiceOver and NVDA.

Open questions (to resolve in grooming session)
---
- Should expansion state be persisted per-user? Pro: reduces repeated discovery cost. Con: adds sync complexity and cross-device inconsistency.
- How many groups should be visible in compact view before we collapse to a single overflow? (3–6?)
- Do we allow third-party links (external deep links) to open in full-page by default? Security considerations.

Next steps (short-term roadmap)
---
1) Spike: client-side compact rail prototype + keyboard interactions (1 week) — frontend
2) Spike: resolver API + basic popularity scoring (1 week) — infra
3) Align on landing UI content and copy with content design (2 days) — PM + Content
4) Usability test plan + recruit (2 weeks) — UX Research

Appendix: sample micro-copy snippets
---
- 404 landing message: "We couldn't find that page. Try these recent models or search by ID."
- Permission denied row: "You don't currently have access. Request access or view a public example."
- Recover CTA: "Open most recent matching deployment" (secondary: "Search all models")

Slack refs / links seen in research
---
- #console-ux thread: "compact-rail-testing" (2024-08-30)
- #sre: "deep-links-on-failover" (2024-09-05)

Notes-to-self
---
- keep wireframes lightweight (svg + annotated frames) and attach to RW-4789.
- coordinate with solutions eng for permission flow edge cases (they often need impersonation stories).

End.
